planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; install a rhizome barrier since this running bamboo spreads by underground rhizomes.

directions: Walking stick bamboo is a mid-sized timber bamboo prized for the odd, swollen, zigzag-knuckled nodes that develop on canes grown in sun, a trait that made dried culms a traditional material for carved canes and walking sticks. New culms emerge green and mature to a warm olive, with fine evergreen foliage that gives useful screening without the towering scale of larger timber bamboos. Site it where the running rhizomes can be contained, since like most Chimonobambusa it spreads steadily once established in favorable soil. Thin congested culms in late winter to keep clumps open and to encourage the best node swelling on remaining canes.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial shade sheltered from drying wind.

directions: This naturally occurring pink-flowered form of early stachyurus carries the same stiff, arching bare branches lined with drooping chains of bell-shaped late-winter flowers as the typical pale-yellow species, but the blooms open in dusky rose-pink tones instead, giving the late-winter display noticeably warmer color against bare twigs. It is otherwise identical in habit and culture to the species, forming a broad, horizontally tiered deciduous shrub that works well at a woodland edge where winter bloom can be viewed from a window. Keep roots cool and evenly moist with a woodland-style mulch, and prune immediately after flowering only, since next year's bloom buds set on the current season's growth by midsummer.
sources: Hillier Manual of Trees and Shrubs

planting.note: Divide and plant in spring into gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; established clumps resent root disturbance, so divide only when necessary.

directions: Broad-leaved snow tussock forms a dense, arching mound of glossy, strap-like evergreen foliage that catches light beautifully and stays tidy without the coarse bulk of its larger New Zealand tussock-grass relatives. In summer, creamy-white plumed flower spikes rise well above the foliage mound, aging to a soft buff tan that persists into winter for extended seasonal interest. It performs best with sharp drainage and resents being waterlogged over winter, making a raised bed, gravel garden, or coastal border ideal settings. Comb out old dead foliage by hand each spring rather than cutting back hard, since the crown can rot if cut too low.

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in lean, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; avoid rich fertilizer, which encourages lanky growth at the expense of flowering.

directions: One of the oldest and most widely grown Correa hybrids, Mannii is a long-lived cross between the red-flowered and white-flowered native fuchsia species, producing abundant pendulous, tubular orange-red flowers through the cooler months when little else blooms in mild-winter gardens. Its dense, rounded, small-leaved evergreen habit makes a reliable informal hedge or background shrub that tolerates coastal wind, salt spray, and considerable neglect once roots are established. Give it sharp drainage and avoid summer irrigation on established plants, since wet feet in heavy soil are its main vulnerability. Light tip-pruning after the main winter-spring bloom keeps growth dense rather than open and straggly.
